brief:
Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat who runs the Board of Peace charged with delivering President Trump's Gaza plan, responded on Sunday to two days of Israeli strikes that killed civilians and destroyed medical stockpiles — in a statement that does not name Israel, the Israeli military, or any author of the strikes at all, anywhere in its text.

"Two days of strikes across Gaza have killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies that people depend on," Mladenov wrote on X, in remarks carried by the Times of Israel and the Anadolu agency. The strikes, he continued, came after intense efforts by the Board and the mediators — Egypt, Türkiye, Qatar and the United States — to bring the Palestinian factions to agree to a roadmap for implementing the plan, handing over civilian governance and decommissioning their weapons. "Both parties carry obligations," he wrote, adding that his team was "working around the clock with the parties, the mediators and regional partners to de-escalate," and that lasting peace was "hard but achievable if everyone makes their best efforts."

![What the statement says, and what the record says](times-of-palestine-mladenov-grammar-2026.svg)

Read the sentences the way an editor would. The strikes arrive in the text the way weather arrives — "across Gaza," from nowhere, killing without a killer. The obligations belong to "both parties," distributed evenly between the side flying the aircraft and the side being bombed. The effort required belongs to "everyone," which is the diplomatic spelling of no one. In the same seventy-two hours this newspaper has documented, Mohammad Dahlan accused Benjamin Netanyahu by name of a massacre committed to kill the ceasefire; Gaza's medics counted at least eighteen dead since Friday, in the toll reported by Al-Monitor; Al Jazeera reported an Israeli strike destroying a medical-supply warehouse; and an Israeli minister told his public plainly that no deal to halt the attacks existed. The one voice institutionally charged with shepherding the peace produced the one statement in which nobody did anything.

The omission is sharpest against the coverage of the statement itself. The Jerusalem Post's headline said the strikes were the IDF's; Israel National News wrote that Mladenov "condemns Israeli strikes." Both supplied, as a matter of routine copy-editing, the word the envoy's own text withheld. When Israeli outlets name Israel more readily than the mediator does, the mediator's grammar is itself news.

There is a professional defence of that grammar, and fairness requires stating it. Mladenov is not a commentator; he needs Israeli cooperation for every clause of the plan he administers, from withdrawal lines to the entry of aid, and a mediator who indicts one side publicly may buy a headline at the cost of the table. His statement did register — Israeli media read it as criticism, and his reference to destroyed medical supplies was widely understood as pointing at the warehouse Israel bombed. The Board's team is, by every account, genuinely working to stop the shooting, and the roadmap the factions accepted on Thursday is largely its work. But Palestinians reading the statement will notice what it costs them specifically: in the envoy's text, the party whose weapons must be decommissioned is named — "the Palestinian factions in Gaza" — while the party whose weapons killed eighteen people this weekend is not named even once. The asymmetry of the language reproduces, in miniature, the asymmetry Palestinians keep being asked to accept in the plan itself. The measure this newspaper set when the first halt was promised remains the only one that matters — not the statements, but the silence of the guns — and by Sunday night it had still not been met.
